newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels, mediators to meet on stalled Peru talks.
newsitem.headline: Rebels, mediators to meet on stalled Peru talks.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 men hostage in Peru expected to meet on Sunday with mediators to discuss resuming stalled talks with the government to end the 82-day crisis despite a gulf of mistrust.
"I expect the (guarantors) commission will make contact to preserve a new dialogue," rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said on Saturday in a walkie-talkie interview.
He said he could not say if or when the rebels would return to the bargaining table for talks with government negotiators.
"We'll wait for the guarantors commision to come here, talk to them and, at that point, decide," he added. "We are constantly evaluating the situation."

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) last week abruptly broke off talks with the government, charging security forces planned to attack the besieged Japanese ambassador's home via tunnels being dug under the residence.

With negotiations at a standstill, Roman Catholic church officials on Saturday became the latest to urge both sides to resume discussions and avoid bloodshed in ending Latin America's longest hostage siege.
"We can't let it reach the point of violence," Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora, archbishop of Lima and the head of Peru's Catholic Church, told reporters.
Both the rebels and President Alberto Fujimori made statements of their wish to resume talks.
An MRTA spokeswoman said rebels, holed up in the residence since Dec. 17, had heard strange noises for days underneath the building in Lima's upscale San Isidro district.

"We heard noises, not just for a moment but for several days. (At first) we didn't want to go public with this; we waited to find out for sure," said the guerrilla, who identified herself as Comrade Micaela in a two-way radio interview with Reuters.

The 20-odd rebels who stormed the residence almost 12 weeks ago in a hail of bullets and explosions are demanding the release of hundreds of jailed comrades. The government has steadfastly refused to consider the idea.

But talks seeking a bloodless end to the crisis, which restarted Feb. 11 after weeks of being logjammed, were making progress until the MRTA announced it would not attend a 10th round set for last Friday.

Rebels on Saturday suggested a softer line, saying they were "evaluating" the situation and awaiting the arrival of the three-member guarantors commission of mediators. Asked in the radio interview if talks may resume, Micaela said: "We hope so."

Local radio station Radioprogramas del Peru quoted Cerpa as saying, also via two-way radio, that he would probably meet on Sunday with the guarantors, but adding: "We still need to adjust some details" before renewing dialogue.
One commission member, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, visited the besieged residence on Saturday. A Japanese doctor followed.

Fujimori said in a statement on Friday he hoped to resume talks to prevent bloodshed but that all talks were off if the rebels in any way harmed their hostages, including the president's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers and Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

Micaela, one of two women among the rebels, issued the MRTA's salute to International Women's Day with a speech in defence of "outcast and exploited women who fight day after day with their children against (Fujimori's) brutal economic policies."
Fujimori, a divorced father of four, paid his own tribute to International Women's Day by speaking to a mothers' group in a shantytown. He dodged questions about the alleged tunnel.

A poll published on Saturday in a local newspaper but taken before the talks were broken off showed Fujimori's popularity rose some in February. Datum Internacional's survey of 402 Lima residents said Fujimori's popularity rose to 47 percent last month from 43 percent in January, newspaper El Comercio said.

The MRTA issued a statement via its "Rebel Voice" page on the Internet, citing the ill-health of 31 of the rebel prisoners whose release it is seeking. "Most suffer these illnessess as a result of tortures, bad health conditions in the jails and bad diet," the statement said.
